question: Back in the Soviet era, a person studied applied mathematics at a Russian technical university founded in 1971 that trains civil aviation specialists. This person then worked at a Soviet computing center in the early 1980s—a facility founded in the mid-1950s as the first academic computing facility in the Soviet Union, located in the capital city, named after its founding director who served from 1955 to 1989, operating as part of a scientific organization affiliated with the Ministry of Science and Higher Education, and currently directed by an academician. Using a Soviet minicomputer released in 1978 that displayed text characters instead of graphics, this person developed puzzle games, and later contributed to the puzzle design of a 1992 tile-matching video game featuring a character from a popular Nintendo franchise, co-designed by the creator of Tetris. This person is the creator of a globally popular puzzle game. Under Soviet state property laws, the intellectual property rights to this game were automatically acquired by a state-controlled Soviet foreign trade organization that was established in the early 1970s and held a monopoly over international electronics transactions during the Cold War. This organization was led by a director during pivotal international licensing negotiations in the late 1980s. That director later privatized a major Soviet state organization during the dissolution of the Soviet Union in the early 1990s, and also led an American technology company that held patents for safety devices including handheld fire extinguishing equipment and was involved in a legal dispute in the early 2010s related to intellectual property management. Additionally, that director filed and won a significant business lawsuit in America in the early 2010s against individuals who were found by a court to have committed fraud and breach of fiduciary duty against a business partner in an international case involving R-Amtech International. Those individuals were ordered to pay several million dollars in financial penalties following a multi-week trial at the largest trial court in Washington state, and one of them, an attorney, resigned from professional practice in lieu of discipline in the late 2010s due to misconduct findings from that case. Finally, this organization was acquired in the mid-2000s by a video game company founded in 1996 that serves as the exclusive worldwide licensor for that popular puzzle game brand. What was the name of this Soviet foreign trade organization?

The fungus itself was discovered in the upper reaches of a river flowing through a non-flooded, nutrient-poor Amazonian forest, growing on decaying plant material. It has small basidiomata with an olivaceous brown pileus and emits green luminescence from both pileus and mycelium. It is the third documented luminescent member of the family Mycenaceae from the Amazon. What is the full name of this newly described luminescent fungus species?

Consider the world's most extensive astronomical glass plate collection, containing over 550,000 negatives documenting over 150 years of observations. This collection is housed at an organization that also employed over 146 women astronomical computers from the 1880s to the 1960s, who studied these plates and made significant discoveries. The collection itself was the subject of a two-decade digitization effort led by a professor who holds the Robert Treat Paine Professor of Practical Astronomy title, completing in the early 2020s after scanning over 450,000 plates. Its founding was funded by a 19th-century woman astronomer who established a memorial fund in 1886, creating the Henry Draper Memorial as its core. The collection also features contemporary artistic interpretations, including works by an associate professor of art studio at a women's college who created monuments honoring historical women astronomers. The organization maintains modern research initiatives: a searchable digital platform connecting over 428,000 plates with more than 2,500 notebooks created by pioneering women scientists, and a project focusing on historical notebooks. This project utilizes crowdsourcing through a platform started in 2013 that has engaged over 56,000 volunteers for transcription work, and employs a global citizen science platform with over a million volunteers to identify non-textual items through its "Star Notes" initiative, which completed Phase 1 in mid-2022. The project makes its transcriptions searchable on a system operated by a research institute founded in 1890 under a NASA cooperative agreement. This system maintains three bibliographic databases containing more than 13 million records covering astronomy, physics, and arXiv e-prints, and is expanding beyond its original focus to include additional science domains under an initiative per NASA request.

Now, an astronomer from this organization authored a paper documenting a celestial object with a perfect halo of approximately 17 arc seconds in radius surrounding a central image. This discovery was published in a peer-reviewed monthly publication founded in 1849 and owned by the American Astronomical Society since 1941, in the mid-20th century. The findings challenged standard galaxy formation theories and suggested dark matter can be separated from galaxies, with updates published in mid-2021.
